sections.question: What policy changes, government announcements and implementation evidence concern immigration across the public record since July 2024?
sections.answer:
Since July 2024, the public record shows a range of immigration policy changes and implementation evidence. The Department of Home Affairs reported delivering measures in 2024-25 focused on "strengthening the integrity and quality of the international education sector," including a new ministerial direction and changes to the visa application charge. On 31 July 2024, the business innovation and investment program was closed to new applicants, and the new national innovation visa and skills-in-demand visa were implemented on 7 December 2024. A new core skills pathway and specialist skills pathway were implemented on 8 December 2024, and the Pacific engagement visa was rolled out via a ballot on 18 July 2025 to Tuvaluans. The department also noted it is working with the ATO on a data-matching program for temporary skilled visa holders to detect underpayment and exploitation, and is developing the essential skills visa pathway for lower paid workers.

In July 2024, the Government implemented a pilot to strengthen reporting protections for temporary visa holders, including international students, co-designed with unions and civil society organisations. This was part of a package of reforms to address migrant worker exploitation announced in June 2023. In 2024, the Migration Amendment (Strengthening Employer Compliance) Act introduced three new work-related offences addressing coercive practices used by employers to exploit migrant workers, and in March 2025 a $13.25 million grant program was launched to educate temporary visa holders and their employers about the reforms. The Migration (Public Interest Criterion 4022—Code of Behaviour) Instrument 2025 requires certain visa holders to sign an enforceable code of behaviour, where breach could lead to visa cancellation, immigration detention or reduction in income support; the committee noted this replicates the 2024 version of the code and raised human rights concerns.

On the legislative front, Senate divisions on 28 November 2024 show votes on the Migration Amendment Bill 2024, Migration Amendment (Removal and Other Measures) Bill 2024, and Migration Amendment (Prohibiting Items in Immigration Detention Facilities) Bill 2024. The Migration Amendment (Strengthening Sponsorship and Nomination Processes) Bill 2024 lapsed before the election, and the measures in the current bill do not include provisions from the 2024 bill on streamlining labour market testing and indexation of income thresholds. In December 2023, the government reduced the number of required advertisements from three to two and removed the need to advertise on the Workforce Australia website, and in December 2024 the Department of Home Affairs revised regulations to establish income thresholds and their annual indexation for the 'skills in demand' visa. The core skills occupation lists came into effect on 7 December 2024, and the department reported 164,860 applications in the skills-in-demand visa subclass in 2024-25 compared to 121,168 previously.

sections.question: What do bills, government releases, contracts, grants and disclosure records reveal about immigration, and what remains unproven since July 2024?
sections.answer:
The parliamentary record since July 2024 shows repeated Senate and House divisions on migration-related bills and regulations, with the government and opposition generally voting together against Greens and crossbench amendments. On 3 July 2024 the Senate voted 11–27 against disallowing the Migration Amendment (Graduate Visas) Regulations 2024, meaning the regulations remained in force; Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi described them as "yet another cruel blow to international students." On 14 August 2024 the Senate voted 12–26 against disallowing the Migration Amendment (Visa Application Charges) Regulations 2024. On 28 November 2024 the Senate passed the Migration Amendment Bill 2024 and related bills at second and third reading (26–12 and 26–13 respectively), rejecting amendments from Senator Thorpe (14–24), the Australian Greens (12–26), and Pauline Hanson's One Nation (3–32). The House of Representatives had earlier agreed to the bill's second reading on 20 November 2024 by 50–9. On 6 February 2025 the Senate voted 17–29 against referring the Migration Amendment (Prohibiting Items in Immigration Detention Facilities) Bill 2024 to a committee for inquiry.

The record also shows a House vote on 6 November 2024 rejecting Liberal MP Dan Tehan's amendments on excluded occupations to the Migration Amendment (Strengthening Sponsorship and Nomination Processes) Bill 2024, 63–78. A Senate division on 28 November 2024 on business rearrangement, which included Senator Malcolm Roberts criticising "record immigration" and rising housing and rental prices, was lost 32–33. These are votes and procedural outcomes; they do not by themselves prove the effects claimed in debate. No passage provides evidence of actual delivery, payment, or implementation outcomes for any migration measure, nor does any record establish a causal link between immigration policy and housing or cost-of-living changes. Political characterisations, such as the Greens calling the migration package "one of the most extreme changes in migration policy since White Australia," are attributed claims made in debate, not established facts.

In the Senate on 28 November 2024, the three migration bills passed their second reading 25–13 and third reading 26–13, with the Noes in both divisions being the Greens senators Sarah Hanson-Young, Larissa Waters, Peter Whish-Wilson, Nick McKim, Jordon Steele-John, Mehreen Faruqi, Dorinda Cox, Penny Allman-Payne, Fatima Payman, Barbara Pocock, David Shoebridge and Steph Hodgins-May, joined at third reading by David Pocock. Earlier that day, the Senate rejected Senator Thorpe's second reading amendment to withdraw the Migration Amendment (Removal and Other Measures) Bill 2024, which stated the bill "raises significant human rights concerns, including breaking Australia's human rights obligations as a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention"; the amendment failed 14–24, with the Ayes being the same Greens cohort plus David Pocock and Tammy Tyrrell. The Senate also rejected Pauline Hanson's One Nation amendment on sheet 2619, which noted the bill did not "solve the problem of removing non-citizens from immigration detention", by 3–32, with only Malcolm Roberts, Ralph Babet and David Pocock supporting it.

In debate, Greens senators and MPs criticised the major parties on asylum policy. One Greens senator said "refugee and migrant rights are under constant attack in this country, with unlawful indefinite detention and offshore processing remaining in place for asylum seekers; this government introducing laws to strip asylum seekers of due process; and the opposition wanting to strip benefits from temporary residents". Another Greens senator claimed "pretty much every time" Labor had passed "the most hateful laws against asylum seekers", citing mandatory detention and the Nauru deals, and was rebuked for interjecting. A Greens MP said "our humanitarian obligations here in this place must also ensure that we're upholding our obligations to protect and promote the rights of refugees, asylum seekers and people who are stateless", and that "in the last parliament we saw both of the major parties demonise migrants". A Labor-aligned speaker criticised the former Coalition government, saying the then minister Dutton had renewed Paladin's Nauru contract despite breaches, and that "in 2022 the Nauru offshore processing contracts cost the taxpayers $485 million despite there being just 22 refugees and asylum seekers there". Another senator noted "offshore detention emerged during a period of toxic politics" and that "while the agreement with Nauru endures, there is no current agreement with PNG, despite Australia still being responsible for the refugees held there". A senator who said they had introduced a private member's bill "to end indefinite detention of asylum seekers and children" also described the migration bill as "another step in that slow creep towards stripping away rights of asylum seekers in this country", calling offshore detention "a system that the UK government toyed with copying from us but abandoned, because it was just too inhumane".

Separately, in estimates hearings in 2025 and 2026, senators pressed the Department of Home Affairs on unanswered questions about asylum seekers transferred to regional processing countries, including whether the department accepted the UN Human Rights Committee's finding that Australia "remained responsible for the arbitrary detention of asylum seekers redirected or transferred to offshore detention facilities". One senator noted the UN committee had ruled in January 2025 on two cases brought by people held on Nauru. Another senator complained that a question on notice from 4 November 2024 about "the breakdown of people seeking asylum who've been transferred to Australia from offshore detention" remained unanswered "one year and three months" later.

sections.question: What has been said about immigration levels and skilled migration since July 2024?
sections.answer:
In Australian Parliament estimates hearings from 2025, government representatives and senators discussed immigration levels extensively. A departmental official detailed key migration measures delivered in 2024-25, including closing the business innovation and investment program to new applicants on 31 July 2024, implementing the new national innovation visa and skills-in-demand visa on 7 December 2024, and rolling out the Pacific engagement visa via a ballot on 18 July 2025. The official also noted the core skills occupation lists came into effect on 7 December 2024, and that the skills-in-demand visa saw 164,860 applications in 2024-25 compared to 121,168 previously.

Senators raised concerns about migration numbers and targeting. One senator stated that net overseas migration for the year up to 31 March 2025 was 315,900, which they said was "46 per cent higher than the 10-year average before the COVID-19 pandemic" and "34 per cent higher than the long-term assumption used by the Centre for Population." Another senator claimed that analysis showed just 20 per cent of 301,000 net overseas migrants in 2025 were skilled, and criticised the skilled list for including occupations such as dog handler, hairdresser, gardener, golfer and migration agent. A different senator asserted that net permanent and long-term immigration to May 2025 was 246,000 people, "a record for the first five months of the year," and cited a Deloitte report finding that 44 per cent of permanent migrants are underutilised.

Government representatives defended the migration program. One minister said net overseas migration had fallen for six consecutive quarters in annual terms and was "over 40 per cent down on its peak," adding that it peaked at 538,000 in 2022-23 based on inherited policy settings. Another minister stated that net overseas migration was 306,000 in 2024-25, down from its post-COVID high, with temporary students being the largest group of migrant arrivals at some 157,000 people. A minister also argued that census data shows Australia does not have record levels of immigration, and that migration is critical for maintaining quality of life and supporting essential services like aged, child and health care. Government representatives also noted that the 2025-26 permanent migration program had not been announced as of mid-August 2025, with one senator raising this as an issue causing problems for applicants in the skilled stream.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Community safety and immigration?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary debate shows community safety and immigration were repeatedly linked, with several speakers claiming the Albanese Labor government had failed on both. One opposition member asserted the Minister for Home Affairs had "failed" to fix the immigration system, noting that more than 18 months after parliament created the community safety order regime, "the minister has still not lodged a single application for a preventive detention order," despite the member for Scullin promising in May last year that six applications were nearly ready and a further 26 were in the advanced stage of preparation. Another speaker claimed the government's "direction 99 debacle" saw "97 criminal noncitizens avoid deportation" and that the Minister for Home Affairs had been "personally interviewing Palestinian families before granting them humanitarian visas," while thousands of tourist visas were granted to people in a war zone before ASIO checks. A further opposition member said Iran had "fertile ground to plant and grow its hatred in Australia" because current immigration policy allows people who nurture such hatreds to come here, and claimed Labor had given "3,000 people from Gaza permission to come here" as "3,000 potential agents for the Iranian revolutionary guard."

Government and crossbench speakers defended the need for integrity and safeguards. One speaker said communities "deserve a migration system built on integrity at its core," with "clear rules, consistent enforcement and decisions that are made in Australia's national interest," but added that "strong powers must come with strong safeguards" and "ministerial discretion must be exercised transparently and responsibly." Another acknowledged the NZYQ cohort following the High Court's 2023 decision, stating some members "have committed serious crimes" and that it is "absolutely appropriate to ensure we have measures to keep our community safe," while criticising "rushed legislation and a rushed response." A Victorian minister rejected a motion on immigration and community safety as divisive, saying "no multicultural community is served by polarisation and division" and accusing the federal Liberal Party of using a global crisis "to inflame tensions and sow fear," while noting ISIS persecuted Muslims too and that "the vast majority of ISIS victims overseas were Muslim." One speaker also noted that "confusing and legitimate concerns in the community about high immigration" with racism is "wrong," while another said "First Peoples do not use immigrants and refugees as political footballs" and that "no colonial government in this country has the right to say who and who isn't illegal on stolen land."

sections.question: What has parliament said about Lunar New Year and immigration?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary records show Lunar New Year is widely celebrated as a multicultural event, with motions and statements in New South Wales and Victoria acknowledging its cultural and religious significance. In NSW, the Legislative Council noted celebrations hosted by the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office on 27 January 2025 and a Buddhist Blessing Ceremony in Cabramatta on 16 February 2025, commending organisers for fostering cultural understanding and community harmony. A NSW minister also described Lunar New Year as "a major fixture on NSW's cultural calendar." In Victoria, a minister said the state is "home to those celebrations and vibrant and diverse communities," and a federal MP noted Melbourne's Chinatown as "the oldest continuous Chinese settlement in the Western world."

On immigration, the record is limited and comes from attributed political claims rather than settled findings. A federal minister, responding to a question, said migrants "have made an essential contribution, not just to our economy but to our society," and that the government welcomes people who call Australia home. The same minister criticised the Opposition for demanding urgent action on gun laws after an antisemitic attack, saying the Opposition had shifted from demanding immediate legislation to arguing it was rushed. Separately, an opposition MP claimed the Minister for Home Affairs had failed to lodge a single application for a preventive detention order under the community safety order regime, despite promises that applications were nearly ready—a characterisation of the minister's performance, not an established fact.

sections.question: What has parliament said about Bondi Beach attack and immigration?
sections.answer:
Parliamentary records show that, in response to the Bondi Beach attack, the Parliament passed the "Combatting Antisemitism, Hate and Extremism (Criminal and Migration Laws) Act 2026" on 20 January 2026. The Act "included reforms to Australia's migration laws to improve community safety by enabling the Minister for Home Affairs to refuse to grant, or to cancel a visa, on the basis of hate motivated conduct and offences relating to the spread of hatred and extremism." A Senate committee later commented on this bill and the related firearms bill, noting they were "introduced and passed after the massacre at Bondi Beach where 15 people died and many more were injured at a Jewish festival on 14 December 2025."

The record also contains political statements about immigration and the attack. One speaker, identified as a member of the Nationals, criticised political figures who "pander" to far-right voters or "try to out-Pauline Pauline Hanson," and quoted Hanson as saying "there are no good Muslims," calling that statement "hatred" and "vilification." The same speaker also referenced calls for "the deportation of Australian citizens because of their religion, their skin colour or their cultural identity" as an example of extremist behaviour being encouraged. These are attributed claims by that member, not established facts.

sections.question: What has parliament said about the Multicultural Victoria Amendment Bill 2026?
sections.answer:
The Victorian Parliament debated the Multicultural Victoria Amendment Bill 2026, which would abolish the Victorian Multicultural Commission and replace it with a new statutory entity, Multicultural Victoria, led by a multicultural coordinator general and two deputies. The bill implements recommendations from the 2025 Victorian multicultural review led by George Lekakis AO. The Coalition did not oppose the bill's second reading but moved amendments, including that any coordinator general or deputy appointed before 30 January 2027 finishes on that date, and raised concerns about recruitment beginning before the bill was introduced, the lack of a guaranteed dedicated workforce or operating budget, and the need for meaningful multifaith representation. The Libertarian Party opposed the bill, arguing the government should not interfere in communities and criticising the establishment of LanguageLoop as a preferred provider, which it said would undermine market diversity for interpreters and translators.

Government members strongly supported the bill. One member said Victoria is "the most successful and vibrant multicultural society in the world" and that the bill establishes "a renewed, modernised and deeply accountable foundation" for engaging with multicultural and multifaith communities. Another said the bill strengthens institutions and ensures community voices sit at the centre of government decision-making. The Greens supported the bill but argued it "does not go anywhere near enough" and criticised that it "does not even mention racism or discrimination." The Greens also condemned a lack of consultation with the language services sector and proposed amendments, including requiring cabinet submissions to include a multicultural impact statement and enabling the advisory group to obtain information about reported racism and hate incidents. Legalise Cannabis Victoria supported the bill. The bill was later included in a government business program motion to be considered and completed by 5 pm on 13 August 2026, and it was also listed in a Scrutiny of Acts and Regulations Committee Alert Digest.

eras.label: 1993–2009
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on immigration between 1993 and 2009? The debates of the period included Australian Citizenship Amendment (Citizenship Testing) Bill 2007, Auditor-General’s Reports and Migration Amendment (Abolishing Detention Debt) Bill 2009.
eras.answer:
The parliamentary record from this period shows immigration policy developing through two main legislative debates. On the **Australian Citizenship Amendment (Citizenship Testing) Bill 2007**, speakers debated the introduction of a citizenship test for prospective migrants. One member noted the bill had "been of some controversy in the western suburbs of Adelaide" and sought to address local concerns. The Chair of the Senate Standing Committee on Legal and Constitutional Affairs, Senator Barnett, reported that the committee had brought down a report in July 2007 and acknowledged "the minister's response to that report and the recommendations in it." The committee later recommended "that the operation of the citizenship testing regime be reviewed three years after the bill's commencement," particularly to assess its impact on refugee and humanitarian entrants.

On the **Migration Amendment (Abolishing Detention Debt) Bill 2009**, the Rudd government proposed removing "the liability for detention and related costs for certain persons, and liable third parties" and extinguishing "all outstanding immigration detention debts." Government speakers framed this as part of "a broader reform of immigration detention," arguing it corrected "a significant social injustice" and made Australia no longer "the only country in the world that charges innocent people the cost of incarcerating them." The bill retained detention debt liability for "convicted illegal foreign fishers and people smugglers," whom the government characterised as "operating for the sole purpose of making money." Opposition speakers opposed the bill, with one senator claiming the government's legislative priorities were politically motivated; a government senator characterised this opposition as having "an ulterior motive" and being "a foolish course of action."

The record also shows debate over process and political tactics. One opposition senator moved to discharge the detention debt bill from the Notice Paper, but the Greens opposed that motion, stating "this piece of legislation should be dealt with and should be kept on the Notice Paper." A government senator criticised the opposition for gagging debate and for not listing certain government bills as urgent, including the detention debt bill and a political donations bill. The record does not establish any direct causal link between political connections and policy outcomes; it only reports the claims and positions of individual speakers.

eras.label: 2010–2019
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on immigration between 2010 and 2019? The debates of the period included Harmony Day and Racism.
eras.answer:
Immigration and multiculturalism were debated in the context of Harmony Day and opposition to proposed changes to section 18C of the Racial Discrimination Act. A federal MP from Perth, in a speech supporting a motion on Harmony Day, described his electorate as having "very strong migrant communities" and praised their contribution to the "richness, vibrancy and diversity of Perth". He also criticised the then Prime Minister for introducing an amendment to weaken section 18C on Harmony Day, calling it "short-sighted, divisive" and accusing the Liberal Party of "appeasement policy towards Pauline Hanson 2.0". Another federal MP, co-chair of the Parliamentary Friends of Multiculturalism, recounted co-hosting an interfaith dialogue for Harmony Day with the member for Macmillan, involving the Grand Mufti of Australia and the Chaldean Catholic Bishop, where speakers acknowledged "Australia is largely a successful multicultural society".

In the New South Wales Parliament, the shadow Minister for Multiculturalism, a Labor member, spoke about Harmony Day events and called on the Berejiklian Government to "stand up to its Federal counterparts and stop the changes to the Racial Discrimination Act", urging the Premier to follow former Premiers O'Farrell and Baird in rejecting the changes. A motion by Dr Mehreen Faruqi was agreed to, noting that 21 March is the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination and Harmony Day, and that "many people in New South Wales still experience both everyday and institutionalised racism, especially Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people". The motion reaffirmed the House's commitment to "stamping out racism". A federal senator from the Australian Greens also asked the Prime Minister, on Harmony Day, why he had chosen that day to "weaken protections against racist hate speech". One speaker, reflecting on immigration policy, noted Australia had "longstanding bipartisan immigration policy" since the post-war years, described as "arguably the best in the world", while another acknowledged "my own party's history of support for the White Australia policy, right up to the 1960s, is part of that story".

eras.label: 2020–2024
eras.question: How did policy and public debate develop on immigration between 2020 and the middle of 2024? The debates of the period included South Australian Multicultural Bill, Multicultural Grants Program and Afghanistan.
eras.answer:
The South Australian Multicultural Bill 2020 was introduced by the Marshall Liberal government to modernise the South Australian Multicultural Ethnic Affairs Commission Act 1980. The bill proposed replacing the South Australian Multicultural and Ethnic Affairs Commission with the South Australian Multicultural Commission, removing the word "ethnic" from the legislation, and incorporating the concept of "interculturalism" for the first time in Australian legislation. The bill also provided for a South Australian Multicultural Charter, described as "the centrepiece of this particular piece of legislation," which would set out fundamental principles defining multiculturalism and interculturalism for all South Australians. The legislation was enacted as the South Australian Multicultural Act 2021 on 2 December 2021, and the Multicultural Charter was launched by the Premier and the Minister for Multicultural Affairs.

During debate, the opposition raised concerns about the bill. The opposition's lead speaker noted that the opposition held eight Zoom forums and more than 20 meetings with community leaders, and expressed concerns about "a perceived weakening of the functions of the commission." The opposition filed amendments on three matters that were not agreed to: recognising the contribution of temporary migration, raising awareness of the harm of racism as a function of the commission, and requiring state authorities to report on performance of the charter to the minister with the report tabled in parliament. One opposition member also questioned whether proper consultation had occurred with diverse Aboriginal communities in South Australia, given the bill's references to Aboriginal peoples and its definition of interculturalism, citing comments from Noel Pearson about constitutional recognition. The Assistant Minister to the Premier, Jing Lee, stated that the government had introduced a public call for expressions of interest for new commission members commencing 1 July 2021, saying this was "the first time a government in South Australia has introduced expressions of interest."

On the Multicultural Grants Program, the record states that the program was promoted through email distribution to more than 1,500 multicultural contacts, on the multicultural affairs website and GRANTassist website, and via social media platforms Facebook, Twitter and LinkedIn. Projects funded under the program were publicly available on the multicultural affairs website. The Assistant Minister described four grant lines introduced since 2018: Advance Together for capacity building, Celebrate Together for events, Expand Together for equipment and infrastructure, and Stronger Together for service delivery. A Connect Together grant was introduced during the COVID period to help organisations rebuild confidence.

On Afghanistan, the record is limited to a brief exchange in which a minister stated that the Minister for Immigration, Citizenship, Migrant Services and Multicultural Affairs and the minister were "working very closely with local communities here in Australia" to understand issues relating to people who had been in Afghanistan and were either on their way to Australia or had just arrived, and that the minister for immigration was "taking a leading role in that."

key_moments.title: Australian Citizenship Bill 2005; Australian Citizenship (Transitionals and Consequentials) Bill 2005
key_moments.speaker: Ian Campbell
key_moments.brief: The Australian Citizenship Bill 2005 was introduced to replace the 1948 Act, retaining citizenship as a privilege and adding a four-year lawful residence requirement (including 12 months as a permanent resident), mandatory refusal for security threats, identity verification, and new revocation grounds, with several recommendations from the Senate committee adopted. The companion Australian Citizenship (Transitionals and Consequentials) Bill 2005 implements transitional arrangements, including applying the new residence rules only to future permanent residents and registering adoptions under the Hague Convention.

key_moments.title: Migration Amendment (Notification Review) Bill 2008
key_moments.speaker: Stephen Conroy
key_moments.brief: The Migration Amendment (Notification Review) Bill 2008 was introduced to clarify how the Department of Immigration, Migration Review Tribunal, and Refugee Review Tribunal communicate with clients. It aims to address notification defects that have caused court challenges, unlawful detention, and large legacy caseloads, including changes regarding minors, substantial compliance with notification content, and deemed versus actual receipt.

key_moments.title: Asylum Seekers
key_moments.speaker: Jenny Leong
key_moments.brief: Ms Leong condemned both Labor and Liberal governments for operating offshore detention centres on Manus Island and Nauru, noting that about 600 asylum seekers have been transferred there and subjected to inhumane conditions without food, water or sanitation, contravening Australia's obligations under the United Nations refugee convention. She argued that only The Greens support bringing all refugees to Australia, and commended protesters and young Labor activists for raising human rights concerns.

lede.text: Immigration is fundamentally a contest over how Australia balances border control, humanitarian obligations and economic need, with one side defending firm enforcement and another warning that security measures can erode rights and multicultural cohesion. In the current parliamentary fight, Labor and Coalition senators secured passage of the 2024 migration bills, while Greens and crossbenchers opposed them as threats to refugee rights, due process and Australia’s multicultural character. The immediate struggle is over migration’s scale and composition, as critics connect high numbers with housing pressure, while ministers emphasise that net overseas migration has fallen more than 40 per cent from its peak. Across the longer arc, debate has moved from confidence in multicultural contribution and detention reform toward sharper disputes over citizenship, removal, offshore processing, skilled selection and the social consequences of population growth.
